Title: Vehicle-to-grid power fundamentals: Calculating capacity and net revenue
Abstract: As the light vehicle fleet moves to electric drive (hybrid, battery, and fuel cell vehicles), an opportunity opens for “vehicle-to-grid” (V2G) power. This article defines the three vehicle types that can produce V2G power, and the power markets they can sell into. V2G only makes sense if the vehicle and power market are matched. For example, V2G appears to be unsuitable for baseload power—the constant round-the-clock electricity supply—because baseload power can be provided more cheaply by large generators, as it is today. Rather, V2G's greatest near-term promise is for quick-response, high-value electric services. These quick-response electric services are purchased to balance constant fluctuations in load and to adapt to unexpected equipment failures; they account for 5–10% of electric cost—$ 12 billion per year in the US. This article develops equations to calculate the capacity for grid power from three types of electric drive vehicles. These equations are applied to evaluate revenue and costs for these vehicles to supply electricity to three electric markets (peak power, spinning reserves, and regulation). The results suggest that the engineering rationale and economic motivation for V2G power are compelling. The societal advantages of developing V2G include an additional revenue stream for cleaner vehicles, increased stability and reliability of the electric grid, lower electric system costs, and eventually, inexpensive storage and backup for renewable electricity.

Title: Is awareness of public charging associated with consumer interest in plug-in electric vehicles?
Abstract: Policymakers often seek to increase the visibility of plug-in electric vehicle (PEV) chargers in public locations in effort to build familiarity and interest in PEVs. However, it is not clear if the visibility of public charging stations actually has an impact on PEV demand. The purposes of the present study are to (1) assess the current levels of visibility for public PEV charging infrastructure within Canada and (2) identify whether or not a statistically significant relationship exists between consumer awareness of public charging infrastructure and interest in purchasing a PEV. We use data collected from a sample of 1739 Canadian new-vehicle buyers in 2013. About 18% of Canadian respondents have seen at least one public charger, while the proportion is highest in British Columbia (31%). We find a significant bivariate relationship between public charger awareness and PEV interest. However, when controlling for multiple explanatory variables in regression analyses, the relationship is weak or non-existent. While perceived existence of at least one charger exhibits no significant relationship with PEV interest, perceived existence of multiple chargers can have a weak but significant relationship. Thus, public charger awareness is not a strong predictor of PEV interest; other variables are more important, such as the availability of level 1 (110/120-volt) charging at home.

gold.abstract: This paper investigates the economic impact of vehicle-home-grid integration, by proposing an online energy management algorithm that optimizes energy flows between an electric vehicle (EV), a household, and the electrical grid. The algorithm leverages vehicle-to-home (V2H) for self-consumption and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) for energy trading, adapting to real-time conditions through a hybrid long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network for accurate household load prediction, alongside a comprehensive nonlinear battery degradation model accounting for both cycle and calendar aging. Simulation results reveal significant economic advantages: compared to smart unidirectional charging, the proposed method yields an annual economic benefit of up to EUR 3046.81, despite a modest 1.96% increase in battery degradation. Even under unfavorable market conditions, where V2G energy selling generates no revenue, V2H alone ensures yearly savings of EUR 425.48. A systematic sensitivity analysis investigates how variations in battery capacity, household load, and price ratios affect economic outcomes, confirming the consistent benefits of bidirectional energy exchange. These findings highlight the potential of EVs as active energy nodes, enabling sustainable energy management and cost-effective battery usage in real-world conditions.

These are your colleagues' latest proposals:

--- Researcher B ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper-b contributes V2G capacity and net revenue equations for electric-drive vehicles across peak power, spinning reserves, and regulation markets, showing near-term economic value in high-value quick-response services. Paper-c contributes survey evidence from 1,739 Canadian new-vehicle buyers that public charger awareness is weakly or non-significantly related to PEV interest after controls, while home charging availability is more important.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
The operational link is economic reframing: paper-b’s V2G revenue calculations can turn public charger visibility from a passive familiarity cue into an active revenue signal. If charger awareness alone has weak effects on PEV interest (paper-c), adding a quantified V2G revenue stream may strengthen interest by addressing economic motivations rather than mere visibility. The causal chain is: awareness of V2G-enabled public chargers → perceived personal revenue from grid services → increased PEV purchase interest.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
A randomized survey experiment with Canadian new-vehicle buyers. Conditions: (1) control, (2) public charger awareness only, (3) V2G-enabled charger awareness with a revenue estimate calculated from paper-b’s equations for a representative PEV supplying regulation and spinning reserves. Measure PEV interest, perceived economic benefit, home charging access, and demographics. Use regression models mirroring paper-c’s controls. Validate revenue estimates through sensitivity analysis on market prices and vehicle parameters. Missing cross-paper knowledge: paper-b’s revenue equations are not calibrated to Canadian markets or V2G-enabled public chargers; paper-c did not measure V2G awareness or revenue expectations.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
We test whether adding V2G revenue estimates to public charger awareness increases PEV interest more than charger visibility alone. Building on paper-b’s V2G revenue calculations and paper-c’s finding that charger awareness weakly predicts PEV interest, we propose an experiment reframing public chargers as income-generating grid assets. This would identify whether economic incentives can overcome the weak awareness effect observed in Canada and inform infrastructure communication policy.

FINAL IDEA: Public charger awareness may weakly predict PEV interest, but adding V2G revenue estimates derived from grid-service capacity calculations could transform charger visibility into an economic incentive that strengthens consumer interest.

--- Researcher C ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
Paper-b contributes engineering-economic equations to calculate V2G capacity and net revenue for three EV types across peak power, spinning reserves, and regulation markets; it finds V2G most viable for quick-response, high-value services.  
Paper-c contributes survey/regression evidence from 1,739 Canadian new-vehicle buyers that public charger awareness is weak or non-existent as a predictor of PEV interest, while home Level 1 charging availability is stronger.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Use Paper-b’s revenue equations to create a quantified V2G economic benefit treatment. Combine this with Paper-c’s consumer-survey framework. The causal link: Paper-b supplies a missing economic value signal, while Paper-c shows infrastructure awareness alone is weak. We hypothesize V2G revenue information will increase PEV interest only when charging access—especially home charging—is perceived as available, because discharging requires reliable plug-in access. Missing cross-paper knowledge: neither source measured consumer response to V2G revenue or bidirectional charger awareness.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
2x2 factorial survey experiment with Canadian new-vehicle buyers. Factor 1: charger awareness—standard public charger measure from Paper-c versus V2G-capable public bidirectional charger. Factor 2: V2G revenue information—annual net revenue calculated from Paper-b equations for regulation/spinning reserves for a typical battery EV versus no revenue. Outcome: PEV purchase interest using Paper-c’s Likert scale. Controls: home charging availability, demographics, commute, environmental attitudes. Validation: revenue figures derived from Paper-b formulas; manipulation check for revenue recall; control arm should replicate Paper-c’s weak charger-awareness finding. Test interaction: revenue effect stronger among respondents with home charging.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
This project tests whether quantified V2G revenue, calculated from vehicle-to-grid engineering-economic models, interacts with charging-infrastructure awareness to shape PEV demand. Using a survey experiment with Canadian buyers, we vary exposure to V2G-capable public chargers and annual V2G revenue information. We expect revenue information to increase PEV interest mainly among households with home charging access, providing behavioral demand evidence to complement engineering V2G cost calculations.

FINAL IDEA: Testing whether adding engineering-calculated V2G net revenue to public charging awareness increases PEV purchase interest, conditional on home charging access.
